title: Rejecting extremism
hook: scholars have condemned terrorism as against Islam, as in the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi

segments.voice: Yesterday, Islamic finance today: trade permitted, riba forbidden, and an honest argument about the difference. Your line was finance without interest. Who owned what, in the product you looked up? Today, a harder question, and a new week. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

The letter is addressed to one man, by name. Not to the world, not to the press, but to Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, the man who had declared himself caliph of the group called ISIS, and to the fighters who followed him. It's written in Arabic, in the language of the law he claimed to be applying. And it's signed by Muslim scholars and leaders from many countries. Its message, point after point, is a single word: no. Today, rejecting extremism, and what it looks like when scholars answer violence with their own texts.
screen: `ADDRESSED TO ONE MAN.` → `WRITTEN IN HIS OWN TERMS.` → `ONE WORD: NO.`

segments.voice: The Open Letter to al-Baghdadi doesn't shout. It argues, verse by verse, like a teacher marking an exam. It says that issuing religious rulings without the learning they require is forbidden. That killing the innocent is forbidden. That killing emissaries is forbidden, and so killing journalists and aid workers is too. That torture is forbidden. That declaring other Muslims to be unbelievers, when they haven't declared it themselves, is forbidden. And that fighting in Islam has rules, a right cause and a right conduct, and isn't permitted without them. Behind those points sit texts anyone can read. In Surah al-Baqarah, Pickthall: "Fight in the way of Allah against those who fight against you, but begin not hostilities. Lo! Allah loveth not aggressors." And in Sunan an-Nasa'i the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, warns against going to extremes in religion, saying, in paraphrase, that people before you were destroyed by it. The Arabic word is ghuluw: overshooting, going past the mark. Read beside the letter, the hadith names the charge. Not too much religion. Excess that leaves religion behind. The letter is one statement among several. Scholars in different countries have issued their own fatwas and declarations against terrorism, in mosques and in print. They are public, and anyone can read them. And they say, in their own words, what today's line says in three.
screen: `AN ARGUMENT, POINT BY POINT.` · `BEGIN NOT HOSTILITIES.` · `GHULUW: GOING PAST THE MARK.` · `SIGNED, DATED, AND PUBLIC.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read a scholars' statement, but first, make room for it. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a headline that used a faith's name for an act of violence. You don't have to replay the images. Just notice how the story usually ends there. Now add the part that rarely gets told: somewhere, a scholar sat down and wrote an answer. Hold the line from al-Baqarah: begin not hostilities. If you pray, you can pray for those harmed in that faith's name. If you don't, simply hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Rejecting extremism. Scholars answering violence done in Islam's name with the Qur'an and hadith, as in the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi. Today's word.

Your line: scholars said no. Today, find the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi or another scholars' statement, and read its summary, start to finish. Tomorrow, killing innocents. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Muslim scholars and organizations issue public letters, fatwas and declarations against terrorism, often arguing from the Qur'an and hadith point by point, and imams address the subject in sermons.

fork.setup: you're a scholar. a man has declared himself caliph, and his fighters kill journalists and aid workers in your faith's name. what do you do?
options: stay quiet: it isn't your fight.
write to him by name, in Arabic, and answer him point by point from the texts.
issue a short statement in English for the press only.
fork.reveal: the signers of the Open Letter wrote to al-Baghdadi by name, in Arabic, and argued from the Qur'an and hadith that what his group was doing is forbidden.

original.note: Arabic: excess, overshooting the mark; the word in the hadith warning against extremes in religion.

trapdoor: what you thought: Muslim scholars stay silent about terrorism.
what it means: scholars have answered it publicly, as in the Open Letter to al-Baghdadi, point by point from the texts.
what a scholar hears: 2:190 behind the argument; the hadith on ghuluw in an-Nasa'i; and a letter that argues on the group's own legal ground rather than around it.

notes: The outline gives the letter's year (2014) and calls the scholars 'worldwide'; the script omits the year and says 'scholars and leaders from many countries' to keep to the claims rule. Confirm against the letter's text and signatory list.

The letter's points are paraphrased from its executive summary as recalled (no fatwa without learning; no killing the innocent; no killing emissaries, so journalists and aid workers; no torture; no takfir without open disbelief; jihad has rules). Check each against the published summary.
'Scholars in different countries have issued their own fatwas and declarations against terrorism' is stated without naming them; a Keeper may add named examples.
Confirm Pickthall's wording for 2:190 exactly as quoted.
Confirm hadith number an-Nasa'i 3057 (also Ibn Majah 3029) and the gloss of ghuluw as 'going past the mark'.
Handled with care: names ISIS and al-Baghdadi only as the letter does; no images, no attack details.
